newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FCC chief against fees for Internet firms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FCC chief against fees for Internet firms.

text.p: The nation's top communications regulator reiterated Wednesday that he is against imposing on Internet-access firms the existing system of access charges paid by long-distance phone companies.

But Federal Communications Commission Chairman Reed Hundt also told a conference that his agency will have to replace the current access charge system with a new system that does the same thing and is applied to telecommunications providers in a "competitively neutral" way. The existing access charge system plays a key role in funding universal phone service.

Hundt also suggested the possibility that his agency's upcoming rules on funding universal phone service might include a provision to finance hooking up all the classrooms in the country to the Internet.
"We should spend what it takes," he told reporters after a speech to a conference sponsored by the Wall Street Journal newspaper.
Hundt added that he believes such a project probably would cost less than the $5 billion to $10 billion estimates now circulating.
Speaking about access charges, Hundt said he supports reforming the access charge system as opposed to taking the existing system and applying it to Internet-access companies.
Hundt noted that with Internet usage taking off, some people are calling on the FCC to subject Internet service providers to the access charges now paid by long-distance carriers.

"You don't pour new wine in old bottles and if we applied these old access rules to new technologies, you'd have every reason to whine," he said. "Instead, let's just break the old bottleneck of access."
Hundt also reiterated that he opposes subjecting Internet telephony to the same rules that apply to conventional phone service.
"I hope the FCC bars any state from limiting the growth of Internet telephony," he said. "We want states to regulate less, not more."
